text:
The cyberpunk metropolis glowed with neon, its skyscrapers a constellation of light against the night. Below, the streets thrummed with the pulse of hovercars and the constant churn of humanity, all under the watchful eyes of omnipresent digital billboards.

In this hyper-technological sprawl, where data streams flow as freely as the smog-choked air and corporate logos eclipse the stars, the concept of a candle is an archaic relic, a whisper of a pre-digital age. Yet, in the dimly lit backrooms of underground jazz clubs or the private sanctuaries of high-ranking executives seeking to disconnect from the neural net, a candle still burns. Its primary material is wax, specifically paraffin wax, a byproduct of petroleum refining that serves as a stark, ironic symbol in a city built on the very fossil fuels that once powered the industrial revolution. This wax is often blended with stearic acid to harden the structure, allowing it to stand tall against the humid, acid-rain-soaked winds that buffet the lower districts. The wick, typically braided cotton, acts as the conduit for the flame, a tiny, flickering rebellion against the cold, unblinking LEDs that dominate the skyline. The scent of burning paraffin, sharp and chemical, mixes with the ozone and exhaust of the city, creating a sensory dissonance that reminds those who smell it of a time when light was something earned through friction and fire, not something downloaded or streamed.
